title: Reading Question Types, Solved
subtitle: A practical guide to timing, skimming and the main IELTS Academic Reading question types
description: This ebook teaches you how to manage your time across three passages and handle the most common Academic Reading question types. Each chapter gives a clear method, short examples and a self-check task.
audience: Learners aiming for Band 6 to 7 in Academic IELTS Reading who want a clear method for each question type.

chapters.title: Start Here: How the Reading Test Works
chapters.summary: A quick map of the test, the question types, and how to use this book.
chapters.body:
The Academic Reading test lasts 60 minutes. It has 40 questions across three passages. There is no extra time to copy your answers, so you must write them on the answer sheet as you go, or save a few minutes at the end. This single fact shapes everything in this book.

The passages usually become harder from the first to the third. They come from books, journals, magazines and newspapers, and they are written for a general reader. You do not need special knowledge of science or history. Every answer is in the text. Your job is to find it, not to know it.

## The question types in this book

Each passage brings two or three groups of questions. You will meet these types again and again:

- True/False/Not Given, which tests whether you can match a statement to the writer's claim.
- Matching headings, where you choose a heading for each paragraph or section.
- Multiple choice, with one correct answer among several options.
- Sentence and summary completion, where you fill gaps using words from the passage.
- Matching information, where you find which paragraph contains a detail.

Each type rewards a different habit. That is why we study them one by one.

## Why many Band 5 and 6 learners get stuck

Most learners at this level do not fail because their English is too weak. They fail because of habits. They read every word of the passage slowly. They spend ten minutes on one hard question. They choose an answer because a word "looks the same" in the text. They never check why they lost marks.

Think of a Dhaka bus journey during rush hour. You cannot look at every shop on the road. You watch for your stop. Reading for IELTS is similar. You need landmarks, not every detail.

Example: A learner reads the first passage word by word and finishes it in 28 minutes. She now has only 32 minutes for two harder passages. Her English is good, but her plan is poor. A better plan would have saved her at least ten minutes.

## How to use this book

Each chapter teaches one skill. Read the chapter, then do the short exercise at the end. Use a real passage from a practice book or a past paper for the exercise, and always time yourself. Reading about technique is not enough. You must practise it under a clock.

Keep a small notebook. We will call it your error log. After every practice passage, write down the questions you missed and the reason. Chapter 7 shows you how to turn this notebook into a revision plan. Start it today, even if you only write one line.

Tip: Do not try to learn all the question types in one week. Practise one type for two or three days, then move on. Deep practice beats quick reading.

## A realistic goal

A higher band is not magic. It comes from many small gains: five more seconds saved on each scan, one fewer careless spelling mistake, one clearer decision on a True/False/Not Given item. Nobody can promise a score, but steady, honest practice improves your accuracy and your confidence.

Before you read on, take one passage and time how long you need to read it normally. Write the number down. You will compare it with a new number at the end of the book.
takeaways: The test is 60 minutes, 40 questions, three passages, with no extra time to transfer answers.
All answers are in the text; you do not need outside knowledge.
Most lost marks come from habits, not weak English.
Start an error log today.
chapters.exercise: Time yourself reading one passage the way you normally do, and write down the minutes. Then list which of the five question types you find hardest.

chapters.title: Time Management Across Three Passages
chapters.summary: Plan your 60 minutes so no single passage or question steals your score.
chapters.body:
You have 60 minutes for 40 questions. If you divide the time equally, each passage gets about 20 minutes. This is a good starting point, but it is not a rule you must follow like a robot. Many learners find the first passage easier and the third harder. A flexible plan works better.

## A simple timing plan

Try this as a base plan:

- Passage 1: about 17 to 18 minutes.
- Passage 2: about 20 minutes.
- Passage 3: about 22 to 23 minutes.

This gives your hardest passage a little more time. It also protects you from the common mistake of spending too long early and then rushing at the end. Because there is no extra transfer time, write your answers on the answer sheet as you work. If you write in the question paper first, move your answers every few minutes, not all at the end.

## The 20-minute passage routine

Inside each passage, use a repeatable routine:

- Two minutes: read the title, the first line of each paragraph, and the last line of the passage. Get the shape of the text.
- Two minutes: read the questions and underline key words.
- Thirteen to fifteen minutes: find and write the answers.
- One minute: check spelling and word limits.

The exact numbers are not holy. The idea is that you always know where you are in the passage and what comes next.

## Rules for hard questions

A hard question is like a load-shedding hour. You cannot fix the power cut by staring at the dark. You light a candle and continue with other work.

Use the same attitude. If you cannot find an answer in about a minute, mark the question with a small circle and move on. Come back if you have time. Never leave a blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so always write something, even a guess.

Example: In Passage 2, question 22 is a True/False/Not Given item that confuses you. You have spent 90 seconds. You circle it, write "NG?" lightly in pencil, and move to question 23. You finish the group, and in the last two minutes you return and decide.

## Know your question order

Most question groups follow the order of the passage. If question 15 is answered in paragraph C, question 16 is usually later in C or in D. This helps you narrow the search area. Matching headings and matching information are exceptions, so treat them separately.

## Practise the clock

Use a watch or phone timer during practice. Write the start time at the top of the page. After each passage, write the finish time. Compare it with the plan. If Passage 1 takes you 25 minutes, find out why. Did you read too closely? Did you chase one difficult item?

Tip: Do one full 60-minute test every week or two. Between full tests, do single passages under a 20-minute timer. Short timed practice builds the habit more easily.

## Stay calm

Panic wastes time. If you notice your heart racing, stop for five seconds. Breathe once. Look at the next question and start again. One bad paragraph is not the end of the test.
takeaways: Start with about 17-18, 20, and 22-23 minutes for the three passages.
Use a routine: skim, read questions, find answers, check.
Circle hard questions after about a minute and return later.
Never leave a blank; write answers on the answer sheet as you go.
chapters.exercise: Do one passage with a 20-minute timer. Write the time you finished and the question numbers you circled and skipped.

chapters.title: Skimming and Scanning: Reading Less to Score More
chapters.summary: Learn two different speeds of reading and when to use each.
chapters.body:
Skimming and scanning are two tools. Many learners mix them up, so let us separate them clearly.

Skimming means reading quickly to get the general idea. You do not read every word. Scanning means looking for one specific thing, such as a name, a number, a date or a key word. You move your eyes over the text until you find it, then you slow down and read that part carefully.

## How to skim a passage

Before you answer any question, spend about two minutes skimming:

- Read the title and any subtitle.
- Read the first sentence of every paragraph. This is often the topic sentence.
- Read the last sentence of the final paragraph, which often gives a conclusion.
- Notice words such as however, but, in contrast and therefore. They show changes in direction.

After this, you should be able to say in one sentence what the passage is about and what each paragraph does. If you cannot, do it again with a pencil, writing two or three words beside each paragraph.

Example: A passage is titled "The return of the urban tree." Paragraph A introduces why cities lost trees. Paragraph B describes a planting project. Paragraph C lists problems. Your quick note might read: A - lost trees, B - project, C - problems. This small map will save you minutes later.

## How to scan for an answer

Scanning starts with the question, not the passage. Follow these steps:

- Choose the key word in the question. Names, numbers, dates and unusual nouns are the easiest to find.
- Think of other ways to say it. If the question says "reduced," the passage may say "fell" or "declined."
- Move your eyes down the paragraph quickly, looking for the key word or its partner.
- When you find it, read the whole sentence before it and after it.

## Capital letters, numbers and shapes

Your eyes can find some words faster than others. Capital letters show names of people and places. Digits show years and quantities. Words in quotation marks stand out. Use these shapes as landmarks. Think of finding a friend in the crowd at Dhaka's New Market: you look for the red shirt, not every face.

## Do not hunt for the same word only

A common trap is searching only for the exact word from the question. IELTS questions usually paraphrase. The question may say "children," and the text may say "young people" or "under-sixteens." Always search for a meaning, not just a spelling.

Tip: When you underline a key word in the question, write a synonym above it in pencil. This trains your mind to look for the idea.

## Common mistakes

- Reading the whole passage slowly before looking at the questions.
- Stopping at the first matching word without reading the full sentence.
- Skimming so fast that you miss negative words such as not, never or hardly.

Speed is useful only when it leads to accurate answers. Skim to understand the structure. Scan to locate. Then read slowly the two or three sentences that matter.

## Build the habit

Choose a short article from a newspaper. Give yourself 90 seconds to skim it, then close it and write two sentences about it. Next, ask a friend to give you five details to scan for. Repeat several times a week. Soon your eyes will move with purpose.
takeaways: Skimming gets the main idea; scanning finds one specific detail.
Read first sentences and note a few words beside each paragraph.
Search for meaning and synonyms, not only the exact word.
After you locate an answer, read the full sentence around it.
chapters.exercise: Skim one passage for two minutes and write a 3-word note beside every paragraph. Then check whether your notes match the main idea.

chapters.title: True/False/Not Given Without the Guesswork
chapters.summary: A clear method for deciding between three answers and avoiding the Not Given trap.
chapters.body:
True/False/Not Given is a favourite worry for learners. The type feels tricky because two answers can look similar. A reliable method turns it into a logical decision.

First, know the meaning of each answer. True means the passage agrees with the statement. False means the passage says the opposite. Not Given means the passage does not say enough to decide. In some tests, you may see Yes/No/Not Given instead. This asks whether the statement agrees with the writer's opinion. The method is the same.

## The four-step method

- Read the statement and underline the key idea. Find the exact claim.
- Scan the passage for the matching sentence. Follow the order of the questions.
- Read that sentence carefully, together with the sentence before and after.
- Compare the meaning of the statement with the meaning of the text. Then choose.

If you find a sentence that says the same thing in different words, choose True. If you find a sentence that directly contradicts the statement, choose False. If you search the right area and find no sentence that answers the exact claim, choose Not Given.

Example: Statement: "Most farmers in the region now use mobile phones to check crop prices." The passage says: "A growing number of farmers have bought mobile phones." The passage does not say "most," and it does not say they check prices. Because the text does not confirm the claim, the answer is Not Given, not True.

## Watch the small words

The difference between answers often sits in one small word. Look for these:

- Quantity words such as all, some, most, few, many.
- Frequency words such as always, often, sometimes, never.
- Strength words such as must, may, might, could.
- Comparison words such as more than, the highest, the first.

If the statement says "all" and the passage says "some," the answer is False if the passage clearly shows that not all do. It is Not Given if the passage says nothing about the rest.

## Do not use your own knowledge

You may know that a fact is true in real life. That does not matter. Your answer must come only from the passage. If you think, "I know this is correct, but the text does not say it," the answer is Not Given.

## The Not Given trap

Learners often choose False when the answer is Not Given. The difference is simple. False needs evidence against the statement. Not Given has no evidence either way. Ask yourself: "Can I point to a sentence that contradicts this?" If you cannot, it is not False.

Tip: For each answer you choose, put a pencil line under the words in the passage that support your decision. For Not Given, write "no info" in the margin. This forces you to think with evidence.

## Practise the decision, not the guess

Do a small set of ten statements and mark why you chose each answer. After checking, study the mistakes. Usually you will find that you ignored a small word or used outside knowledge. Fix that habit and your accuracy will rise.
takeaways: True means agrees, False means contradicts, Not Given means no clear information.
Underline evidence in the passage for every answer.
Watch quantity, frequency and strength words.
Never use outside knowledge to decide.
chapters.exercise: Take five True/False/Not Given statements from a practice test. For each, write the sentence number that supports your answer, or write no info.

chapters.title: Matching Headings and Matching Information
chapters.summary: Two matching tasks that need paragraph-level understanding rather than word-hunting.
chapters.body:
Matching tasks test whether you understand how a passage is built. They are different from detail questions, so they need different habits. Let us look at matching headings first, then matching information.

## Matching headings

In this task, you get a list of headings and several paragraphs or sections. You choose the best heading for each. There are usually more headings than paragraphs, so some headings will not be used.

The main idea of a paragraph is usually in the first or second sentence, and sometimes in the last. Follow this method:

- Read the list of headings first. Underline the key idea in each.
- Read the first two sentences of the paragraph, then the last sentence.
- Ask: what is the paragraph mainly about? Say it in your own words.
- Choose the heading that matches the whole paragraph, not just one detail.

Example: A paragraph begins with a long story about a flood in a village. The final sentences explain how the community built better warning systems. A heading such as "A village disaster" matches the first part only. A heading such as "Improving flood preparation" matches the main purpose. Choose the second.

Be careful with traps. A heading may include a word that appears in the paragraph, but the idea is different. Another heading may be true for only one sentence. The correct heading covers the central message.

Tip: Do the easy paragraphs first and cross out the headings you use. The remaining choices become fewer and your decisions get easier. If a heading is used once, do not use it again.

## Matching information

Here you get a set of statements, and you must find which paragraph contains each one. The paragraph letters are used on the passage margin. The same paragraph may be used more than once, or some paragraphs may not be used. Read the instructions to be sure.

This type does not follow the order of the passage. That makes it slower, so do it after the types that do follow the order, or give it a firm time limit.

Use this method:

- Underline the key idea in each statement.
- Skim each paragraph and write a few words on its content. You may already have this from your skimming notes.
- For each statement, think of paraphrases and scan the likely paragraphs.
- Confirm by reading the sentences carefully. The detail must really be there.

Example: The statement says, "an example of a company changing its working hours." You look for names of companies, times of the day, and words like schedule or shifts. You may find the answer in a paragraph that never uses the word "hours."

## Common problems

- Choosing a paragraph because one word matches, without checking the full idea.
- Spending five minutes on one statement. If it hides from you after a minute, move on.
- Forgetting that a letter can be used again.

Both tasks reward the map you made in the skimming stage. The better your notes, the faster you decide. Make short notes your standard practice.
takeaways: For headings, find the main idea of the whole paragraph, not one detail.
Read the headings first and cross out those you use.
Matching information does not follow passage order; use paragraph notes.
Give hard items a time limit and return later.
chapters.exercise: Choose a passage with matching headings. Write each paragraph's main idea in your own words before looking at the heading list, then match them.

chapters.title: Multiple Choice and Completion Questions
chapters.summary: Handle options, gaps and word limits with care.
chapters.body:
Multiple choice and completion tasks look simple, but they carry many small traps. This chapter shows you how to avoid them.

## Multiple choice

In multiple choice, you read a question and choose from several options. Sometimes you choose one answer; sometimes you choose two or more. Read the instructions carefully.

Do not read the options first and choose the one that "sounds right." Use this order:

- Read the question stem and underline the key words.
- Find the relevant part of the passage by scanning.
- Read that part carefully and decide what the text says in your own words.
- Compare your idea with the options. Remove the options that are clearly wrong.

Wrong options are called distractors. They often use words from the passage, but they change the meaning. One may be too strong, such as saying "always" when the text says "often." One may be true in real life but not stated in the passage. One may mention a detail from another paragraph.

Example: The passage says, "The new bridge was expected to reduce travel time, but traffic increased in the first year." One option says, "The bridge made journeys faster." This uses the idea from the first half, but the text shows that the result was different. It is a distractor.

Tip: Eliminate, then choose. If you can remove two options with confidence, your decision between the last two becomes easier.

## Sentence completion

Here you complete sentences with words from the passage. First look at the word limit, such as "NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS." You must obey it. If the answer is "heavy rain" and the limit is one word, it will be marked wrong. A number may count as a word, depending on the instruction, so read each instruction.

Follow these steps:

- Read the gap sentence and decide what type of word fits: a noun, a verb, a number.
- Scan the passage for the key words around the gap.
- Copy the words exactly as they appear in the passage.
- Read the full sentence to check grammar.

## Summary completion

A summary is a short paragraph with gaps. Some tasks give you a box of words to choose from. Others ask for words from the passage. Read the whole summary first to understand its flow. The summary usually follows the order of the original text, so find where it begins in the passage and move forward.

When a word list is given, remember that there are more words than gaps. Check the part of speech. A gap after "the" is likely a noun or adjective. A gap after "to" may need a verb.

## Spelling and writing

Spelling counts. Copy words from the passage carefully. Write plural forms correctly when needed. Use clear handwriting or capital letters on the answer sheet. Avoid adding extra words, because you may break the limit.

Check each gap sentence by reading it back. If the grammar sounds wrong, you may have chosen the wrong place in the passage.
takeaways: In multiple choice, form your own answer first, then eliminate distractors.
Always obey the word limit exactly.
Copy answers from the passage with correct spelling.
Check that your completed sentence is grammatically correct.
chapters.exercise: Pick one completion task. Before you write the answers, circle the word limit and write the part of speech each gap needs.

chapters.title: Review, Error Log and Your Revision Plan
chapters.summary: Turn every practice test into progress with a simple log and a four-week plan.
chapters.body:
Practice alone does not improve your score. Careful review does. A test you do not review is half finished. This chapter shows how to make mistakes work for you.

## The error log

Use a notebook or a spreadsheet. After every passage, check your answers. For each wrong or guessed answer, write a short entry with these columns:

- Test and passage name.
- Question number and type.
- Your answer and the correct answer.
- The reason you lost the mark.
- What you will do next time.

Be honest about the reason. Use short labels so you can count them later:

- Time: I ran out of time or rushed.
- Vocabulary: I did not know a word or a paraphrase.
- Location: I looked in the wrong part of the passage.
- Meaning: I found the right place but misread it.
- Spelling or limit: I broke the word limit or spelled it wrongly.
- Guess: I had no evidence.

Example: "Passage 2, Q24, True/False/Not Given. I chose False, correct was Not Given. Reason: Meaning. I thought no information meant the opposite. Next time: look for a contradicting sentence before choosing False."

## Find your pattern

After five or six passages, count the labels. You may find that most of your errors are in matching headings, or that most are spelling mistakes. Now you know where to spend your time. A learner who loses marks to spelling does not need more speed training. A learner who loses marks to location needs better scanning.

## Learn vocabulary from the passages

When you meet an unknown word, do not only write its meaning. Note the paraphrase pair. For example, "increase" and "rise," or "cause" and "lead to." Review these pairs once a week. Paraphrase knowledge is one of the strongest tools for this test.

## A four-week revision plan

Adjust this plan to your own schedule, such as around work, university or the weekend.

- Week 1: Review chapters 1 to 3. Do three timed passages. Practise skimming and scanning every day for ten minutes.
- Week 2: Focus on True/False/Not Given and matching tasks. Do four sets of statements and log every error.
- Week 3: Focus on multiple choice and completion. Check word limits and spelling. Do one full 60-minute test.
- Week 4: Mixed practice. Do two full tests under exam conditions. Review the error log and fix the top two problems.

Tip: On the day before a practice test, do not study new material. Sleep well, drink water, and bring a pencil, an eraser and a watch.

## Return to your first number

In chapter 1 you recorded how long you took to read a passage normally. Do the same now with your new routine. Compare the numbers. Also compare your accuracy. This is your real progress, and it is worth more than any guess about your band.

Keep going. A small improvement each week becomes a big one over a month.
takeaways: Review every test; log the question, the reason and the fix.
Count your error labels to find your biggest weakness.
Record paraphrase pairs, not just single words.
Follow a simple four-week plan and finish with full timed tests.
chapters.exercise: Start your error log now with at least five entries from your latest practice passage. Choose one error label to reduce next week.
